time_raw: Between January and June 1995
C_subpractice_description_raw: PF: The native primary forest is characterized by arboreal species of Lauraceae, Rubiaceae, Melastomataceae, Palmae, Bombacaceae, Euphorbiaceae and Cesalpinaceae, that have a canopy height of about 30 m, and numerous vines and epiphytes.
T_subpractice_description_raw: P: The pasture where cattle graze features grasses and isolated trees
C_land_structure_subpractice_raw: PF: The native primary forest is characterized by arboreal species of Lauraceae, Rubiaceae, Melastomataceae, Palmae, Bombacaceae, Euphorbiaceae and Cesalpinaceae, that have a canopy height of about 30 m, and numerous vines and epiphytes.
T_land_structure_subpractice_raw: P: The pasture where cattle graze features grasses and isolated trees
C_out_exp_design: On each site, a transect was established containing eight baited pitfall traps (1000 ml capacity, 13 cm deep, 11 cm diameter) situated 50 m apart. authors: Greenberg R., Bichier P., Cruz Angon A., Reitsma R.
title: Bird Populations in Shade and Sun Coffee Plantations in Central Guatemala
C_site_id: Sierra de las Minas, Polochic Valley
T_site_id: Sierra de las Minas, Polochic Valley
exp_design: Points were located along approximately 2-km transects which were established as much as possible within a single drainage and elevation zone … Points were located at least 25 m from the edge of the woodlots and 200 m from the nearest point … The distribution of the number of points for each habitat is as follows: sun coffee (28 points in Pueblo Viejo, 82 in Tucurú); Inga (122 Tamahú, 82 Tucurú); Gliricidia (25 Jolomjix, 80 Tucurú); matorral (20 Pueblo Viejo, 57 Tucurú), shade cardamom (55 Pueblo Viejo, 46 Tucurú), forest remnant (50 Tamahú, 21 Tucurú)
time_raw: Most counts in coffee plantations and matorral were surveyed twice: once in period I (January–February 1995) and again in period II (mid-March–mid-April). Forest habitats were surveyed only once during the study
T_subpractice_description_raw: Inga shade coffee: over 45 species of trees were found in the Inga
C_agrof_subpractice_raw: In areas of sun plantations that have trees, the trees are small (5–6 m) and the canopy cover negligible ... Trees are usually trimmed twice each year to maintain a parasol architecture that casts a monolayer of shade (Sanchez Castillo 1994) and to avoid too much humidity, which is believed to promote fungal disease ... In addition to these natural rhythms, shade trees were heavily pruned in approximately half the plantations between the two census periods, substantially reducing shade cover
T_agrof_subpractice_raw: Both shade plantation types are characterized by a low (6–8 m) and relatively open (40–50% cover) canopy (Table 1). Gliricidia plantations are strongly dominated (85%) by the most common tree (vs. 61% for Inga) and show considerably lower vertical structural complexity compared to Inga plantations (within-point Coefficient of Variation [CV] of tree height 5 11% versus 20%, respectively). In areas of sun plantations that have trees, the trees are small (5–6 m) and the canopy cover negligible ... Trees are usually trimmed twice each year to maintain a parasol architecture that casts a monolayer of shade (Sanchez Castillo 1994) and to avoid too much humidity, which is believed to promote fungal disease ... In addition to these natural rhythms, shade trees were heavily pruned in approximately half the plantations between the two census periods, substantially reducing shade cover
C_weed_method_raw: The coffee layer provides few resources for omnivorous or granivorous birds (which dominate matorral) because "weeds" are discouraged through the use of herbicides
T_weed_method_raw: The coffee layer provides few resources for omnivorous or granivorous birds (which dominate matorral) because "weeds" are discouraged through the use of herbicides
C_chem_subpractice_raw: All of the Guatemalan plantations used insecticides (Siguenza personal communication)
T_chem_subpractice_raw: All of the Guatemalan plantations used insecticides (Siguenza personal communication)
T_land_structure_subpractice_raw: Inga shade coffee: over 45 species of trees were found in the Inga
C_out_exp_design: Bird census data are based on fixed radius points counts in a total of 666, 25m fixed radus plots. To avoid basing our analysis on replication over too small an area, we used the mean number of individuals observed over all the points in a single transect
T_out_exp_design: Bird census data are based on fixed radius points counts in a total of 666, 25m fixed radus plots. To avoid basing our analysis on replication over too small an area, we used the mean number of individuals observed over all the points in a single transect

exp_design: Based on aerial photographs from 1996 (and in some cases 1984–1985) we selected all forest patches of more than 1 km2. Of these (approximately 40), we selected 15 areas evenly distributed in the elevational range of 1700–2000 m asl. In a similar manner we selected all agricultural areas of more than 1 km2 from aerial photos from 1967, 1975, and 1984–1985. To be considered an agricultural site, the area had to have been in cultivation on the oldest available aerial photo. On the basis of this initial selection we selected 15 sites that were evenly distributed in the area and in the same elevational range as the forest sites. Finally, we selected all stands (around 20) that appeared to be exotic tree plantations (i.e., dense tree cover in an area that in the oldest aerial photos was treeless). In the field we randomly selected one tree in each of the forest sites in an area that was minimally disturbed by humans (selective logging, beehives, coffee production) and >200 m from the forest edge. In the center of the agricultural sites, we selected a mature shade tree in a home garden with coffee (in one site we found no such home garden, hence n = 14). In the plantations we selected a random tree in the middle of the stand. We selected 7 Cupressus-plantations and six Eucalyptus plantations (n = 13 exotic plantations) to get an even distribution between the two plantation types. (See Supporting Information for a list of the sites and Fig. 1 for the distribution of the sites across the investigated landscape.)

authors: Khan Z.R., Midega C.A.O., Amudavi D.M., Hassanali A., Pickett J.A.
title: On-farm evaluation of the 'push-pull' technology for the control of stemborers and striga weed on maize in western Kenya
exp_design: In each district, 20 farmers were randomly selected from those who had recently adopted the 'push–pull' technology to participate in the study...Each of the farmers had a set of two similar plots, a 'push–pull' plot and a maize monocrop plot, both with same level of striga and soil fertility status at the time of establishment
time_raw: The current study was conducted between 2003 and 2006 in 14 districts in western Kenya...In all the districts, except Trans Nzoia where there is only one cropping season in a year (April–September), the studies covered both the long (March–August) and short (October–January) seasons each year
C_subpractice_description_raw: Maize Monocrop (mm): "Each farmer had a set of two plots, a 'push–pull' and a maize monocrop"
T_subpractice_description_raw: push-pull (pp): "The 'push–pull' plot comprised maize intercropped with desmodium, with three rows of Napier grass (Bana variety) planted around this intercrop at a spacing of 50 cm within and 50 cm between rows."
C_intercrop_subpractice_raw: Maize Monocrop (mm): "Each farmer had a set of two plots, a 'push–pull' and a maize monocrop"
T_intercrop_subpractice_raw: The ‘push–pull’ plot comprised maize intercropped with desmodium, with three rows of Napier grass (Bana variety) planted around this intercrop at a spacing of 50 cm within and 50 cm between rows. The innermost row of Napier grass was spaced 1 m from the first row of maize as is often the practice (Khan et al., 2001). Desmodium was planted in between each row of maize. In both plots maize was planted at inter and intra-row spacing of 75 cm and 30 cm, respectively. The number of seeds planted per hill varied from 2–3 but at 4 weeks after crop emergence thinning was done to one maize plant per hill
C_fert_subpractice_raw: Phosphorus, in form of di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), was applied in each plot at planting at the rate of 60 kg/ha. Nitrogen was applied after thinning of maize, in form of calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), at the rate of 60 kg/ha
T_fert_subpractice_raw: Phosphorus, in form of di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), was applied in each plot at planting at the rate of 60 kg/ha. Nitrogen was applied after thinning of maize, in form of calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), at the rate of 60 kg/ha
C_out_exp_design: Infestation: Stemborer and S. hermonthica infestation levels were assessed non-destructively (once in a cropping season), using methodologies adapted from Khan et al. (2006c,d). At 4 weeks after emergence, 100 maize plants were randomly selected in each plot and tagged for subsequent assessments. At 10 weeks after emergence, the number of tagged plants with characteristic 'window-paned' and 'pin-holed' leaves, and/or deadhearts arising from stemborer larval feeding (Ampofo, 1986) was recorded." Yield: All the maize plants in each plot were then harvested and cobs sundried separately for each plot and farmer. They were then shelled and dried to 12% moisture content and grain weights taken individually for each plot and farmer. Grain weights were then converted into tones/hectare. Maize grain yields in the ‘push–pull’ plots were calculated taking into account the entire plot including area occupied by Napier grass "Similarly, the number of emerged S. hermonthica plants was counted from the tagged plants during the same sampling occasion from within a radius of 15 cm around the base of each plant" Means represent data averages of 20 farmers in each district.

exp_design: Plots were laid out in randomized complete block design, with five replications at Mtwapa and four at Amoyo.
time_raw: The study covered six cropping seasons from October 1992 to August 1995 long rains: April–June, short rains: mid-October–mid-December
T_subpractice_description_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart

Plots were mulched with leucaena leaves, except for one of the 2.25 m plots, and regularly weeded, except for another of the 2.25 m plots.
C_out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994). Fresh pheromone was loaded onto the traps during each moth collection day. Data about the total number of male moths were analysed. Abundance per plot (5 plots per treatment)

Four sampling plots per village (25 x 25 m); each plot sampled six times with monthly repetition (Macuya forest only four times). Insects collected using one Malaise trap, nine pitfall traps in a 5 x 5 m grid, and sweeping net zigzag transects (80 m) per plot, between 6:30-10:30 am, March-August 2009 and February-November 2010. exp_design: To control for local effects, study sites were closely situated in a ~25 km² area representing a variety of land uses and management intensities (Fig. S1); distances between capture sites varied from 27 m (within small forest fragments) to 5 km … We treat each night as an independent sample for statistical analyses
time_raw: Sampling was conducted over 22 nights during November, December, and January 2006 (dry season) and over 22 nights during May, June, and August 2007 (wet season)

T_land_structure_subpractice_raw: MMC (Medium-management coffee) commertial polyculture. medium-management plantations had a shade canopy of intermediate diversity and structural complexity
C_out_exp_design:
We recorded bats in forest fragments and in coffee plantations 
of differing diversity and density of shade trees; these plantations 
represented the greatest possible range of management intensities 
in the area...recording time was always similar to time spent 
mist-netting at each site (1800 h to 0400 hours in the dry season, 
and 1800 h to 0200 h in the wet season), with recording 
suspended during high winds or heavy rain. We recorded for an 
average of 8.861.6 SD hours per night. Sampling was conducted 
over 22 nights during November, December, and January 2006 
(dry season) and over 22 nights during May, June, and August 
2007 (wet season)...we collected 11 nights of data in forest fragments, 12 in 
low-management coffee, 11 in medium-management coffee, and 
10 in high-management coffee...We used acoustic monitoring equipment to record echolocation
calls of bats...We captured bats with mist 
nets and identified bats as described in Williams-Guille´n & 
Perfecto

time_raw: Sampling was conducted over 22 nights during November, December, and January 2006 (dry season) and over 22 nights during May, June, and August 2007 (wet season)

C_out_exp_design:
We recorded bats in forest fragments and in coffee plantations 
of differing diversity and density of shade trees; these plantations 
represented the greatest possible range of management intensities 
in the area...recording time was always similar to time spent 
mist-netting at each site (1800 h to 0400 hours in the dry season, 
and 1800 h to 0200 h in the wet season), with recording 
suspended during high winds or heavy rain. We recorded for an 
average of 8.861.6 SD hours per night. Sampling was conducted 
over 22 nights during November, December, and January 2006 
(dry season) and over 22 nights during May, June, and August 
2007 (wet season)...we collected 11 nights of data in forest fragments, 12 in 
low-management coffee, 11 in medium-management coffee, and 
10 in high-management coffee...We used acoustic monitoring equipment to record echolocation
calls of bats...We captured bats with mist 
nets and identified bats as described in Williams-Guille´n & 
Perfecto

title: On-farm evaluation of the 'push-pull' technology for the control of stemborers and striga weed on maize in western Kenya
exp_design: In each district, 20 farmers were randomly selected from those who had recently adopted the 'push–pull' technology to participate in the study...Each of the farmers had a set of two similar plots, a 'push–pull' plot and a maize monocrop plot, both with same level of striga and soil fertility status at the time of establishment
time_raw: The current study was conducted between 2003 and 2006 in 14 districts in western Kenya...In all the districts, except Trans Nzoia where there is only one cropping season in a year (April–September), the studies covered both the long (March–August) and short (October–January) seasons each year
C_subpractice_description_raw: Maize Monocrop (mm): "Each farmer had a set of two plots, a 'push–pull' and a maize monocrop"
T_subpractice_description_raw: push-pull (pp): "The 'push–pull' plot comprised maize intercropped with desmodium, with three rows of Napier grass (Bana variety) planted around this intercrop at a spacing of 50 cm within and 50 cm between rows."
C_intercrop_subpractice_raw: Maize Monocrop (mm): "Each farmer had a set of two plots, a 'push–pull' and a maize monocrop"
T_intercrop_subpractice_raw: The ‘push–pull’ plot comprised maize intercropped with desmodium, with three rows of Napier grass (Bana variety) planted around this intercrop at a spacing of 50 cm within and 50 cm between rows. The innermost row of Napier grass was spaced 1 m from the first row of maize as is often the practice (Khan et al., 2001). Desmodium was planted in between each row of maize. In both plots maize was planted at inter and intra-row spacing of 75 cm and 30 cm, respectively. The number of seeds planted per hill varied from 2–3 but at 4 weeks after crop emergence thinning was done to one maize plant per hill
C_fert_subpractice_raw: Phosphorus, in form of di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), was applied in each plot at planting at the rate of 60 kg/ha. Nitrogen was applied after thinning of maize, in form of calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), at the rate of 60 kg/ha
T_fert_subpractice_raw: Phosphorus, in form of di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), was applied in each plot at planting at the rate of 60 kg/ha. Nitrogen was applied after thinning of maize, in form of calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), at the rate of 60 kg/ha
C_out_exp_design: Infestation: Stemborer and S. hermonthica infestation levels were assessed non-destructively (once in a cropping season), using methodologies adapted from Khan et al. (2006c,d). At 4 weeks after emergence, 100 maize plants were randomly selected in each plot and tagged for subsequent assessments. At 10 weeks after emergence, the number of tagged plants with characteristic 'window-paned' and 'pin-holed' leaves, and/or deadhearts arising from stemborer larval feeding (Ampofo, 1986) was recorded." Yield: All the maize plants in each plot were then harvested and cobs sundried separately for each plot and farmer. They were then shelled and dried to 12% moisture content and grain weights taken individually for each plot and farmer. Grain weights were then converted into tones/hectare. Maize grain yields in the ‘push–pull’ plots were calculated taking into account the entire plot including area occupied by Napier grass "Similarly, the number of emerged S. hermonthica plants was counted from the tagged plants during the same sampling occasion from within a radius of 15 cm around the base of each plant" Means represent data averages of 20 farmers in each district.

C_out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). exp_design: In each district, 20 farmers were randomly selected from those who had recently adopted the 'push–pull' technology to participate in the study...Each of the farmers had a set of two similar plots, a 'push–pull' plot and a maize monocrop plot, both with same level of striga and soil fertility status at the time of establishment
time_raw: The current study was conducted between 2003 and 2006 in 14 districts in western Kenya...In all the districts, except Trans Nzoia where there is only one cropping season in a year (April–September), the studies covered both the long (March–August) and short (October–January) seasons each year
C_subpractice_description_raw: Maize Monocrop (mm): "Each farmer had a set of two plots, a 'push–pull' and a maize monocrop"
T_subpractice_description_raw: push-pull (pp): "The 'push–pull' plot comprised maize intercropped with desmodium, with three rows of Napier grass (Bana variety) planted around this intercrop at a spacing of 50 cm within and 50 cm between rows."
C_intercrop_subpractice_raw: Maize Monocrop (mm): "Each farmer had a set of two plots, a 'push–pull' and a maize monocrop"
T_intercrop_subpractice_raw: The ‘push–pull’ plot comprised maize intercropped with desmodium, with three rows of Napier grass (Bana variety) planted around this intercrop at a spacing of 50 cm within and 50 cm between rows. The innermost row of Napier grass was spaced 1 m from the first row of maize as is often the practice (Khan et al., 2001). Desmodium was planted in between each row of maize. In both plots maize was planted at inter and intra-row spacing of 75 cm and 30 cm, respectively. The number of seeds planted per hill varied from 2–3 but at 4 weeks after crop emergence thinning was done to one maize plant per hill
C_fert_subpractice_raw: Phosphorus, in form of di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), was applied in each plot at planting at the rate of 60 kg/ha. Nitrogen was applied after thinning of maize, in form of calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), at the rate of 60 kg/ha
T_fert_subpractice_raw: Phosphorus, in form of di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), was applied in each plot at planting at the rate of 60 kg/ha. Nitrogen was applied after thinning of maize, in form of calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), at the rate of 60 kg/ha
C_out_exp_design: Infestation: Stemborer and S. hermonthica infestation levels were assessed non-destructively (once in a cropping season), using methodologies adapted from Khan et al. (2006c,d). At 4 weeks after emergence, 100 maize plants were randomly selected in each plot and tagged for subsequent assessments. At 10 weeks after emergence, the number of tagged plants with characteristic 'window-paned' and 'pin-holed' leaves, and/or deadhearts arising from stemborer larval feeding (Ampofo, 1986) was recorded." Yield: All the maize plants in each plot were then harvested and cobs sundried separately for each plot and farmer. They were then shelled and dried to 12% moisture content and grain weights taken individually for each plot and farmer. Grain weights were then converted into tones/hectare. Maize grain yields in the ‘push–pull’ plots were calculated taking into account the entire plot including area occupied by Napier grass "Similarly, the number of emerged S. hermonthica plants was counted from the tagged plants during the same sampling occasion from within a radius of 15 cm around the base of each plant" Means represent data averages of 20 farmers in each district.
